prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Dots and Boxes on a 4x4 box grid. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(horizontal: np.ndarray, vertical: np.ndarray, capture: np.ndarray) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - The game is Dots and Boxes on a 4x4 grid of boxes. - `horizontal`, `vertical`, and `capture` are 5x5 numpy arrays describing the current state. - All array elements are integers in {-1, 0, 1}. - `horizontal[row, col]` encodes whether the horizontal edge at `(row, col)` has been drawn (0 = not drawn; nonzero = drawn). - `vertical[row, col]` encodes whether the vertical edge at `(row, col)` has been drawn (0 = not drawn; nonzero = drawn). - `capture[row, col]` encodes who owns the box at `(row, col)` (0 = unclaimed; 1 = claimed by you; -1 = claimed by the opponent). - A nonzero value in `horizontal` or `vertical` indicates the edge is already occupied and cannot be played again (the sign indicates which player drew it). # Action / Return Format - Return a string move in the format `'row,col,dir'`. - `row` and `col` identify which edge to draw and must be integers in the range 0-4. - `dir` is the edge orientation: `'H'` for a horizontal edge or `'V'` for a vertical edge. - A move is legal only if the chosen edge is currently empty (its value is 0 in the corresponding array). - When you draw an edge, it becomes occupied by you (set to 1 in the corresponding array). - If drawing the edge completes one or more boxes, those boxes become captured by you (set the corresponding `capture` entries to 1). - If you capture at least one box, you immediately take another turn; otherwise the turn passes to the opponent. - The game ends when all edges are drawn; the winner is the player who captured more boxes. - If you are unsure whether a move completes a box, choose a move that is legal and tends to avoid creating a box with exactly three sides filled (which would allow the opponent to score). # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...

For detecting which orientation the current game uses, I'll check whether the extra column/row of nonzero entries sits in the horizontal or vertical array, defaulting to standard when ambiguous or inconsistent, which naturally happens at the very start of the game.

Now I'm shifting to actual strategy: full brute-force search over a 4x4 box grid (40 possible edges) isn't feasible early on, but becomes tractable as an endgame technique. My plan is to represent the state as a 40-bit mask, then reason about greedily capturing boxes with three sides filled — while being careful about the double-cross strategy for chain control once no other safe moves remain.

I'm working out a minimax approach with memoization over the edge state, where the value represents the score differential for whoever moves next, and captures let the same player continue moving. Since exhaustive search over 40 edges is too costly to start from scratch, I'm considering standard simplifications, like the rule that taking a free box is usually correct unless it sacrifices chain control near the endgame.

A cleaner strategy might split into phases: play safely to control chain parity during the midgame, then switch to exact endgame analysis of chains and loops once no safe moves remain — falling back to alpha-beta with transposition tables and heuristics when the position isn't cleanly decomposable, solving exactly once few edges remain.

I'm working through the precise mechanics of the double-cross move: when I've opened a chain for my opponent, I want to capture all but the last two boxes, leaving them as a declined gift rather than taking the final domino, since sacrificing those two preserves my move advantage for the next chain.

This is the actual double-dealing sacrifice: I stop taking two boxes before the chain ends and instead draw the far edge f, turning the last two boxes into a domino the opponent must take together, forcing them to move again elsewhere. So a useful search heuristic emerges: when captures are available, I only need to consider non-capturing moves that create a new 3-sided box adjacent to an already 3-sided one, since that's what a genuine double-dealing sacrifice looks like.

For loops, the same idea applies but I need to leave four boxes as two separate dominos rather than one — stopping my capture chain earlier so two pairs of 3-sided boxes remain, then drawing the one edge between them that completes neither box but sets up two forced two-box handouts.

So the move generator when captures exist should include all capturing moves plus non-capturing moves that create a 3-sided box adjacent to an already-3-sided box. I'm trying to recall whether there's a simpler characterization — like whether taking every available capture first is always at least as good as skipping one, since if safe (non-creating) moves remain after captures, that's typically optimal.

I'm now testing whether declining a capture in favor of a safe move could ever beat taking it — reasoning through a scenario where capturing box b opens up box c, versus leaving it for the opponent, and concluding capturing generally dominates per Wilson's solver approach. I'm also noting the subtlety of multiple simultaneous capturable chains and whether capture order matters for canonicalizing moves.

For complexity, I'm realizing the full opening search is too deep to solve exactly at 40 plies, so I need to reserve exact solving for endgames with a small number of empty edges (maybe 14-16) and fall back to a heuristic depth-limited search otherwise. I'm estimating that Python can only handle roughly 50k-100k node evaluations per second with bitmask operations, so I'm weighing how transposition tables collapse move-order permutations and whether an 18-empty-edge endgame is tractable within that budget.

I should use alpha-beta with transposition table bounds instead, checking time periodically and falling back to a heuristic if the budget of about 0.7 seconds is exceeded.

For that midgame heuristic: take available captures when safe moves remain afterward, but I need to watch for cases where capturing exhausts all safe moves and pushes us into a long-chain endgame with many empty edges still remaining—meaning I also need a chain-based evaluator, not just the exact solver. So really there are two phases to handle: one where safe moves still exist, and one where they've run out and captures/sacrifices dominate.

While safe moves exist, I should choose among them using chain-parity and long-chain-rule heuristics, ideally searching ahead to the point where safe moves are exhausted and then scoring the position with chain/loop endgame theory. Once no safe moves remain, the position decomposes into chains and loops where opening moves within a component are largely equivalent, so I can canonicalize the choice—opening a chain in the middle splits it into two parts the opponent takes, while opening at the end is generally at least as favorable for the player forced to open.

A key exception is a 2-chain: opening its middle edge (a hard-hearted handout) denies the opponent the double-cross option entirely, versus opening at the end which lets them choose whether to take both boxes or sacrifice two for control. I'm now working through whether middle-opening a 3-chain behaves the same way, tracing how drawing the interior edge affects which boxes become capturable and whether the double-cross choice still exists.

With Phase B positions, though, things get more complex since chains and loops may not be fully disjoint — there can be shared edges or partial structures. I'm categorizing boxes by how many undrawn edges they have (1, 2, 3, or 4) to figure out how any given move affects the surrounding structure.
